propositions.text: Pritam Singh Shah seeks judicial review of Immigration Officer's refusal of his Permanent Residence application on H&C grounds.
Immigration Officer refused Mr. Shah's Permanent Residence application on H&C grounds on November 15, 2018.
The refusal was pursuant to section 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of Immigration Officer's refusal of Permanent Residence on H&C grounds under section 25(1) of the Act, dated November 15, 2018.

propositions.text: The Application for judicial review is dismissed.
The Court sympathizes with the Applicant's circumstances and desire to remain in Canada with family.
The Court's role is to determine if the Officer's decision is reasonable, not to make the decision itself.
The Officer's decision is reasonable, justified, transparent, intelligible, and defensible in law and facts.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses Application, sympathizes with Applicant, but finds Officer's decision reasonable, justified, transparent, and defensible.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah is a 78-year-old Indian citizen whose family arrived in Canada in 2010 and are permanent residents.
Mr. Shah lived with his family in India before 2010 and helped raise his grandchildren, imparting culture and language.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant is a 78-year-old Indian citizen with family in Canada since 2010; he helped raise grandchildren in India.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah's daughter-in-law and youngest grandson returned to India in 2010 to care for him.
Before returning to Canada in 2012, daughter-in-law arranged a caretaker who neglected Mr. Shah, causing isolation and poor health.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant states daughter-in-law and grandson returned to India to care for him; caretaker neglected him causing poor health.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah obtained a multiple entry Temporary Residence Visa on March 26, 2015, valid until January 13, 2025.
The TRV permits stays in Canada up to six months with possible extensions.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant holds a multiple entry TRV valid until 2025 allowing stays up to six months with extensions.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah entered Canada as visitor in April 2017 and applied for Permanent Residence on H&C grounds on June 15, 2017.
Application cited establishment in Canada, family ties, separation impact, frail health, and best interests of grandsons.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant entered Canada April 2017 and applied for Permanent Residence on H&C grounds citing family and health factors.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah arrived again in Canada in February 2018 and has remained due to TRV extension.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant arrived in Canada February 2018 and stayed due to TRV extension.

propositions.text: Applicant's family submitted online interest to sponsor him in 2017 but was not selected.
In January 2019, family attempted another sponsorship interest but program closed before filing.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's family tried to sponsor him online in 2017 and 2019 but were unsuccessful due to selection and program closure.

propositions.text: Officer considered relevant evidence and factors, noted positive factors but found H&C exemption not justified.

paragraphs.summary: Officer considered evidence, noted positives, but found H&C exemption unjustified.

propositions.text: Officer gave positive weight to Mr. Shah's visits to Canada and compliance with immigration regulations.

paragraphs.summary: Officer positively weighed Applicant's visits and compliance with immigration rules.

propositions.text: Officer noted Mr. Shah's investments and pension enable independent living in India.
Officer noted Mr. Shah's son would support him whether in India or Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant financially able to live independently in India and supported by son.

propositions.text: Officer gave little weight to Mr. Shah's continuous residence in Canada since February 2018 as establishment factor.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave little weight to Applicant's recent continuous residence in Canada as establishment.

propositions.text: Officer gave significant positive weight to Mr. Shah's family relationship and lack of relatives in India.

paragraphs.summary: Officer positively weighed Applicant's family ties and absence of relatives in India.

propositions.text: Officer gave little weight to family separation impact due to lack of corroborative evidence of need for support.
Officer noted Mr. Shah passed medical exam for TRV extension and has valid multiple entry visa until 2025.
Officer found little evidence Mr. Shah is unfit to travel or unable to return to India due to age.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave little weight to family separation impact, noting medical fitness, valid visa, and travel ability.

propositions.text: Officer noted oldest grandson is 19 and does not meet 'child' definition for BIOC analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found oldest grandson aged 19 not a 'child' for BIOC analysis.

propositions.text: Officer found little evidence of Mr. Shah's role in younger grandson's life.
Officer concluded younger grandson's basic needs would be met without Mr. Shah.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found little evidence of Applicant's role with younger grandson and needs met without him.

propositions.text: Officer concluded H&C factors globally did not warrant exemption under subsection 25(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Officer concluded H&C factors did not justify exemption under subsection 25(1).

propositions.text: Mr. Shah argues decision is unreasonable due to failure to consider his circumstances as a whole regarding hardship if returned to India.
Mr. Shah argues Officer erred in assessing best interests of younger grandson by ignoring relevant evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues decision unreasonable for ignoring full hardship and best interests of younger grandson evidence.

propositions.text: Standard of review for Officer's H&C decision is reasonableness (Kanthasamy v Canada, 2015 SCC 61).

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review for Officer's H&C decision is reasonableness per Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensible outcomes in facts and law (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9).

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness means decision must be justified, transparent, intelligible, and defensible per Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: The Court must defer to the decision-maker and intervene only if the decision fails the Dunsmuir standard.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states it must defer to the decision-maker and intervene only if the decision fails the Dunsmuir standard.

propositions.text: The H&C Officer failed to consider relevant evidence of hardship from unique circumstances including family dependency, lack of social network, and advanced age.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer failed to consider hardship evidence from his unique circumstances including family dependency and age.

propositions.text: Age and family dependency are important factors in assessing hardship, citing Makarenko and Epstein cases.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah submits age and family dependency are important hardship factors, citing Makarenko and Epstein.

propositions.text: The Officer did not consider evidence holistically, violating Kanthasamy principle, leading to contradictory findings.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer failed holistic evidence consideration per Kanthasamy, causing contradictory findings.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to follow Baker guidance to consider children's best interests with substantial weight and sensitivity.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah submits the Officer ignored Baker's guidance on giving substantial weight to children's best interests.

propositions.text: The Officer ignored evidence of relationship with younger grandson, including photos and letters, and failed to draw reasonable inferences.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer ignored evidence of his relationship with his younger grandson and failed to infer reasonably.

propositions.text: The Officer focused on irrelevant BIOC factors like grandson's access to Canadian services, ignoring relevant ones.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah submits the Officer focused on irrelevant BIOC factors, ignoring relevant ones.

propositions.text: H&C considerations no longer use underserved/disproportionate hardship lens; Officer applied Kanthasamy principles and assessed all factors globally.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Officer properly applied Kanthasamy and assessed all H&C factors globally without error.

propositions.text: Officer noted positive factors like family ties but found lack of evidence for other claims; multiple entry visa permits travel.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent notes the Officer found positive family ties but little evidence for other claims and considered travel visa.

propositions.text: Officer correctly applied law on BIOC, found older grandson not a child, and reasonably assessed younger grandson's best interests.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent submits the Officer correctly applied BIOC law and reasonably assessed the younger grandson's best interests.

propositions.text: Officer's decision is reasonable, transparent, justified, addressed all relevant factors and evidence, and did not err or reweigh evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer's decision reasonable, addressing all factors and evidence without error or reweighing.

propositions.text: Section 25 allows discretionary exemption on humanitarian and compassionate grounds considering best interests of affected child.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Section 25 allows discretionary H&C exemption considering best interests of affected child.

propositions.text: H&C relief is discretionary and exceptional; applicant bears onus to prove exemption justified with sufficient evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains H&C relief is discretionary and exceptional, with applicant bearing onus to prove justification.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy explains relief under section 25 varies by case facts and context.

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy explains that section 25 relief depends on case facts and context, as noted by the Court.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy calls for liberal H&C interpretation weighing all relevant factors, acknowledging some hardship is inevitable and insufficient alone for relief.

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy requires liberal H&C interpretation weighing all factors, recognizing some hardship is inevitable and insufficient alone.

propositions.text: Officer considered and weighed all relevant H&C factors, gave significant weight to family ties, but found little evidence for other claims.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer considered all H&C factors, gave weight to family ties, but found little evidence for other claims.

propositions.text: Officer did not consider factors in isolation or make contradictory findings; findings on family ties and establishment are consistent and supported.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer did not isolate factors or make contradictory findings; family ties and establishment findings are consistent.

propositions.text: Officer considered Mr. Shah's age throughout decision, unlike in Makarenko, and informed assessment by personal circumstances including age.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer considered Mr. Shah's age throughout, unlike in Makarenko, informing the assessment.

propositions.text: Unlike Epstein, Officer found little evidence of dependency or inability to care for self, re-establish or travel.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds that unlike Epstein, the Officer found little evidence of Mr. Shah's dependency or inability to care for himself.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged some hardship from family separation but noted some hardship is inevitable and insufficient alone for H&C relief.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer acknowledged inevitable hardship from separation but that alone does not warrant H&C relief.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy and Baker emphasize assessing the BIOC in H&C applications with well-identified, examined interests

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy and Baker require well-identified and examined BIOC in H&C applications, as stated by prior authority.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah submits the Officer was not alert, alive and sensitive to his younger grandson’s best interests
The Officer assessed the BIOC in light of the evidence presented

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer was not sensitive to his grandson's best interests, but the court finds the Officer assessed BIOC properly.

propositions.text: The Officer set an appropriate BIOC analysis approach for H&C applications in three steps

paragraphs.summary: The Officer established a three-step approach to BIOC analysis in H&C applications.

propositions.text: The Officer determined the younger grandson’s best interests include being with parents and having basic needs met
The Officer noted there was little evidence before him

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found the grandson’s best interests are with parents and basic needs met, noting little evidence was presented.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah submits the Officer did not consider evidence of his close relationship with his grandson
The Officer considered photographs showing the relationship between Mr. Shah and his grandsons

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah claims the Officer ignored relationship evidence, but the court finds the Officer considered photographs of them.

propositions.text: The Officer acknowledged Mr. Shah lived with his younger grandson most of his life
The Officer gave significant positive weight to family ties and relationships with grandsons

paragraphs.summary: The Officer acknowledged Mr. Shah’s cohabitation and gave positive weight to family ties with grandsons.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah argues the Officer should have inferred the younger grandson’s interests from the older grandson’s letter
Onus is on Mr. Shah to establish H&C considerations justify exemption; Officer not required to infer negative impact
The older grandson’s letter did not mention the younger grandson

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues for inference from older grandson’s letter, but court says onus is on Mr. Shah and letter did not mention younger grandson.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah argues Officer focused on irrelevant factors and ignored relevant ones like grandson’s age and cultural role
Officer considered Guidelines factors including grandson’s age and found little evidence needs would not be met without Mr. Shah

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah claims Officer ignored relevant factors, but court finds Officer considered Guidelines and grandson’s age properly.

propositions.text: Officer’s decision is justified, transparent and intelligible
Officer reasonably found exemption from Act requirements not warranted
Officer noted other options for Mr. Shah including sponsorship or Super Visa
Judgment dismisses Application for Judicial Review and no question for certification

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer’s decision justified and dismisses judicial review application with no certification question.
